newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - BA link helps Norway airline fight SAS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BA link helps Norway airline fight SAS.

text.p: Norwegian airline Braathens SAFE, flying in the shadow of big brother SAS for the past 50 years, said on Friday it would fight back by expanding its British Airways-linked frequent flyer programme into Swedish skies.

The announcement came as the small Norwegian carrier launched six daily flights between Oslo and Stockholm, furthering its offensive against Scandinavian Airlines System's (SAS) grip on profitable routes within the Nordic region.

Managing director Erik Braathen said the airline's incentive programme, called the BRACard, would be expanded to include flights on Transwede, a small domestic Swedish airline of which it now owns half.
"We will bring that -- the relationship with British Airways, with the frequent flyer programme...to Sweden," Braathen said in an interview at the company's headquarters at Oslo's Fornebu airport.
The BRACard, on which passengers can redeem points in British Airway's programme, will be introduced for Transwede flights later this year or early next year, Braathen said.

Passengers, especially business travellers, say they are loyal to SAS because of its extensive EuroBonus frequent flyer programme, which is linked to its German partner Deutsche Lufthansa AG and U.S. carrier United Airlines.
Braathens SAFE said its plans for Transwede were to set up a sound financial structure.
"First of all our intention is to get firm ground under our feet -- to make sure that we negotiate the various agreements so we get a good footing in terms of the cost structure.
"The airline has been going through four different ownership structures and seven different managing directors, so there are certain things to be ironed out," he said.
Next Braathens planned to hit the Swedish market to improve the profitability on the five routes within Sweden where Transwede operated.
"Secondly, it's to go out and sell in the marketplace so that we make those five routes profitable. Then we'll take it from there."
Braathen said the airline planned to exercise the option it holds to buy the remaining 50 percent of Transwede, which it must do by the end of 1997.
"The intention is that we will do that. We will use the time until then to evaluate the business," he said.

Braathens SAFE said on Friday its pre-tax profit plummeted to 129 million Norwegian crowns ($20.4 million) in the first nine months of the year from 251 million in the same 1995 period, blaming increased price competition and higher operating costs.
Braathen SAFE's entry with six flights onto the Oslo-Stockholm route, where it says it plans a seventh, has pushed prices down.
SAS has cut its Euro business class ticket price by 540 Swedish crowns ($82) to 3,300 and the price of its EuroTicket, which must be purchased four days in advance, by 100 crowns to 2,900.
Braathen said he was not counting on prices to increase again on the Oslo-Stockholm route, but said he was expecting passenger volumes on that flight to rise.
"I certainly believe we've seen a permanent drop in prices of between 10 to 15 percent depending on which ticket you're talking about.
"We've seen it before when you have a second carrier coming into the route. We anticipate 15 percent growth in passenger volume in 1996 and 1997." ($1=6.3135 Norwegian crown, $1=6.5881 Swedish crown)
